# omni_join_token (Resource)

Manages an Omni join token: the secret a machine presents to register itself with the instance.

The token is baked into installation media and into the machine join configuration, so `omni_installation_media_preset` and the `omni_machine_join_config` data source both take one. Leaving them without a token makes them track whichever token is the instance default, which `omni_default_join_token` sets.

Destroying a token that machines are still using stops those machines from re-registering, so Omni records how many have used it in `use_count`. Omni also refuses to destroy whichever token is currently the instance default: point `omni_default_join_token` at another one first.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# A long-lived token for a provisioning pipeline that mints machines continuously.
resource "omni_join_token" "provisioning" {
  name = "provisioning"
}

# A short-lived one for a single batch of machines. Once the batch has joined, letting the token
# expire stops anything else using it, while the machines that already joined stay connected.
#
# The expiration is an absolute instant, not a lifetime, so this configuration describes the same
# expiry no matter how long after it was written it is applied, and re-applying it changes nothing.
resource "omni_join_token" "batch_2026_q1" {
  name       = "batch-2026-q1"
  expiration = "2026-04-01T00:00:00Z"
}

# An expiry that rolls forward on its own. `time_rotating` moves only when it is due, so the
# expiration below is stable between rotations: every 30 days it jumps to 90 days out, renewing the
# token in place without replacing it or changing its value.
#
# Do not use `timestamp()` here. It changes on every plan, so the token would be renewed on every
# apply and the resource would never be clean.
resource "time_rotating" "fleet_token" {
  rotation_days = 30
}

resource "omni_join_token" "fleet" {
  name = "fleet"

  # 90 days past each rotation, leaving a 60-day overlap in which to re-render whatever boot media
  # or iPXE script carries the token.
  expiration = timeadd(time_rotating.fleet_token.rfc3339, "2160h")
}

# Shutting a token off without destroying it. Revoking stops new machines joining and is reversible;
# destroying is not, and `use_count` says how many machines would lose the ability to re-register.
# Prefer this to backdating `expiration`, which the provider refuses.
resource "omni_join_token" "retired" {
  name    = "retired"
  revoked = true
}

# The token value is the secret a machine presents. Anything it is written into, a kernel command
# line or a boot script, hands the ability to join this instance to whoever can read it.
output "provisioning_token" {
  value     = omni_join_token.provisioning.id
  sensitive = true
}

# `expiration` is the signal to renew before machines stop being able to join.
output "batch_token_expires_at" {
  value = omni_join_token.batch_2026_q1.expiration
}

# Baking a token into installation media, so a machine booted from it joins with that token rather
# than with the instance default.
resource "omni_installation_media_preset" "bare_metal" {
  name       = "bare-metal"
  join_token = omni_join_token.provisioning.id

  machine_labels = {
    source = "provisioning"
  }
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) A human-readable name for the token, shown by `omnictl jointoken list` and the name `omni_machine_join_config` looks a token up by. At most 16 characters, and no control characters, which is what Omni accepts. Immutable: Omni fixes it when the token is created.

### Optional

- `expiration` (String) When the token stops being valid, as an RFC 3339 timestamp (e.g. `2027-01-01T00:00:00Z`). Omni stores an absolute instant rather than a lifetime, so this is the very value it holds: the same configuration always describes the same expiry, however long after it was written it is applied. Changing it renews the token in place rather than replacing it, and removing it stops the token expiring at all. Leave it unset for a token that does not expire.

It must be in the future when it is set or changed; an unchanged expiration that has since passed is kept as is, so an expired token can still be revoked. To take a token out of service without destroying it, set `revoked` instead, which is reversible.

For an expiry that rolls forward, drive it from the `time` provider rather than from `timestamp()`, which changes on every plan and would renew the token on every apply.
- `revoked` (Boolean) Whether the token is revoked. Revoking stops new machines joining with it, without destroying it, and can be undone by setting this back to `false`.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String, Sensitive) The token itself. It is both the resource ID and the secret a machine presents, so treat it as a credential: anything it is written into, such as a kernel command line or a boot script, hands the ability to join this instance to whoever can read it.
- `is_default` (Boolean) Whether this is the instance's default token, the one used by media and join configurations that name no token. Set with `omni_default_join_token`.
- `state` (String) The token's state as Omni reports it. One of: `Unknown`, `Active`, `Revoked`, `Expired`.
- `use_count` (Number) How many machines have joined with this token. Destroying a token with a non-zero count stops those machines from re-registering.

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# A join token is imported by its value, which is also its ID. `omnictl jointoken list` shows it.
terraform import omni_join_token.provisioning w7Ns2nQp6xGJ3bYkR1vTfLzA8cMdHeUq
```
